developments: Ranked by consequence for readers: (1) Proactive personal agents with account access, such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and Instinct, are the month's defining interface. They are documented by Meta's designer and model post, and tested first-hand by the Verge, Mollick, Jones, Vo and Kantrowitz. The tests show genuine catches (expiring credits, calendar conflicts) next to alarming failures: no-click purchases, a near car purchase, wrong doctor numbers, and CAPTCHA walls. Muse is now heading to glasses with training-by-default data use. (2) OS-level agents are arriving, but mostly as promises. Microsoft has shipped MXC containment, while Copilot's local actions and Autopilot remain preview or 'coming months'; independent users rate Autopilot at roughly a 50-60% hit rate. Googlebook ships Gemini features that a reviewer found useful mainly for semantic file search, and Gemini folds Spark tasks into the main chat (Android, paid tiers). (3) Personal context on devices is improving unevenly. Siri AI beats ChatGPT on phone-held context but silently skips sources and drops confirmed details. HomeView switches personal contexts by face without voice ID. Ray-Ban Display goes international and online. (4) A visible privacy backlash against camera glasses is now shaping products and policy: Norway's proposed public-place ban, a Dutch retailer halting sales, and Meta's camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio. (5) On the '2001' question, the evidence leans toward voice as a complement, not a replacement. Alexa Plus excels at voice-made routines but fails at agentic errands. Willison voice-built a feature yet finished by typing. The Plottery study found sliders beat re-prompting, and TaskVM users trusted a structured state view over a conversational agent UI. A randomized study shows voice chats shift opinions while sycophancy shapes how users feel. Live avatars and Guided Vision show voice-plus-camera shipping, with stated limits. Research (Copilot delegation, TaskVM, NN/g context libraries) consistently shows that users over-trust agent output and that oversight and context upkeep fall on users.
missing_perspectives: Accessibility users in their own words: Guided Vision is documented only by Google and Aira, with no blind or low-vision user reports. Non-US users are thin; Norway is the only non-US user or policy angle, and the dots UK/EEA exclusion is noted but not explored. Users outside tech and older users are absent; nearly all hands-on evidence comes from reviewers, developers and power users. Research samples skew to university or tech-company participants. Privacy advocates and regulators speaking directly are missing; their positions arrive only via trade press. Long-term or field data are scarce: there are no usage logs or adoption numbers for Muse, dots or Siri AI beyond vendor claims. There is no independent testing yet of Windows Copilot local actions, Muse on glasses, Gemini Live Avatar pricing or latency, or the Samsung and Nothing glasses. Bystanders recorded by camera glasses are discussed but not heard from.
balance: The accepted set mixes vendor primary sources (Google x6, Microsoft, Meta, and Meta's Muse designer via How I AI), independent journalism and reviews (Verge podcasts x3, MKBHD x2, UploadVR x4, Road to VR, 9to5Google), practitioner experience (Willison, Mollick x2, Witteveen x3, Jones x3, Vo, NN/g's Siri test, Kantrowitz), and research (arXiv x5 and NN/g's study). Vendor claims are generally paired with an independent check: Gemini tasks with 9to5Google, Googlebook with MKBHD, Microsoft hybrid routing with Witteveen and Jones, Muse Wonder with Vo and the Verge, and Live Avatar with Witteveen. Guided Vision is the exception and is labelled as unverified. All three themes have usable evidence: personal context and devices (Siri, HomeView, glasses, Norway, Liminal, NN/g context libraries), computer-use agents (the most heavily covered theme, so further agent items were deferred in favour of glasses and voice items), and voice (Alexa Plus, Willison, the voice persuasion study, avatars, Guided Vision, Plottery, TaskVM). Each piece draws on well over three independent publishers, and written, video and podcast sources all contribute to every piece. Weaknesses: Meta/Muse is heavily represented across sources, which reflects news volume rather than corroboration. Several key failures are single anecdotes. The Grokbot leak is relayed and may appear only as an attributed source_claim.
